Shipping with Context: Why Knowledge Graphs Are Becoming the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery

AI is transforming software development at an extraordinary pace. Developers can generate code, write tests, create documentation, and troubleshoot issues faster than ever before.

Yet for most organizations, the real challenge is no longer generating code.

The harder problem is understanding context.

A piece of generated code does not exist in isolation. It interacts with services, infrastructure, security controls, deployment pipelines, compliance requirements, operational processes, and business objectives. Without understanding those relationships, AI systems may be capable of producing outputs, but they struggle to make reliable decisions.

In his session Shipping with Context: Knowledge Graphs as the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery, Prateek Mittal explored why context is emerging as the next critical layer of enterprise AI and why knowledge graphs are becoming a foundational component of modern software delivery systems.

The Next AI Bottleneck Is Not Model Capability

Over the past few years, the conversation around AI has largely focused on model performance.

Organizations compare models, benchmark reasoning capabilities, and evaluate new generations of large language models.

However, many enterprises are discovering that model quality is no longer the primary limitation.

The real bottleneck is access to organizational context.

Most enterprises operate across dozens or hundreds of systems:

  • CI/CD platforms
  • Security tools
  • Cloud infrastructure
  • Observability platforms
  • Ticketing systems
  • Source control repositories
  • Incident management platforms
  • Cost management tools

Each system contains valuable information.

The challenge is that this information remains fragmented.

An AI assistant may understand how to write code, but it often lacks visibility into which services are affected by that code, which teams own those services, what policies apply to them, and what business risks might be introduced by a deployment.

Without context, intelligence remains limited.

Why Enterprise AI Struggles With Context

The problem is not simply a lack of data.

Most organizations already have enormous amounts of operational information available.

The challenge is that this information exists inside disconnected systems.

As Mittal explained, enterprise AI initiatives frequently encounter four common obstacles.

Data Silos

Critical information is distributed across numerous platforms and tools.

Even when the data exists, it is often inaccessible to AI systems or difficult to connect across domains.

Missing Domain Knowledge

General-purpose language models understand public information but typically lack awareness of company-specific terminology, workflows, ownership structures, and operational practices.

This creates a gap between what AI knows and what an organization actually needs.

Hallucination Risk

When models lack context, they compensate by making assumptions.

These assumptions can produce inaccurate recommendations, incorrect conclusions, or actions based on incomplete information.

Governance and Compliance Concerns

Organizations must carefully control how sensitive information is accessed and shared.

Providing AI systems with unrestricted access to enterprise data can introduce security, compliance, and governance risks.

Together, these challenges limit the ability of AI systems to operate effectively in production environments.

The Evolution From AI-Assisted DevOps to AI-Operational DevOps

Many teams are already using AI in their software delivery processes.

Most of these implementations fall into what Mittal describes as AI-assisted DevOps.

In this model, AI helps humans perform tasks such as:

  • Writing code
  • Creating configuration files
  • Generating documentation
  • Producing runbooks
  • Answering operational questions

Humans remain responsible for supplying context, validating outputs, and making final decisions.

This approach delivers productivity gains, but it does not fundamentally change how software delivery operates.

A second model is beginning to emerge.

What Is AI-Operational DevOps?

AI-operational DevOps shifts AI from being a productivity tool to becoming an active participant in delivery workflows.

Instead of requiring humans to manually provide context, AI systems automatically retrieve information from shared enterprise models.

This allows agents to:

  • Evaluate deployment risks
  • Analyze dependencies
  • Simulate outcomes
  • Enforce policies
  • Validate compliance requirements
  • Recommend corrective actions

In this model, context becomes machine-readable rather than conversational.

The system itself becomes responsible for understanding relationships and applying guardrails before actions occur.

This transition requires a shared understanding of the software delivery ecosystem.

That is where knowledge graphs enter the picture.

Understanding the Building Blocks of a Knowledge Graph

A knowledge graph is not simply a database or reporting system.

It is a representation of entities and the relationships between them.

Within a software delivery environment, entities may include:

  • Services
  • Pipelines
  • Deployments
  • Incidents
  • Infrastructure resources
  • Cloud costs
  • Security findings
  • Teams
  • Applications

These entities become nodes within the graph.

The relationships between them become edges.

For example:

  • A service depends on another service
  • A deployment originates from a specific commit
  • A pipeline belongs to a particular team
  • An incident affects a specific application
  • A cloud resource supports a particular workload

Individually, each piece of information has limited value.

Connected together, they create a model that describes how an organization actually operates.

Context Is More Than Data

One of the key ideas presented during the session is that context is not merely information.

Context is information combined with relationships.

Many organizations already collect deployment events, operational metrics, cloud costs, and security findings.

The challenge is that these data points often remain disconnected.

A knowledge graph introduces a semantic layer that allows systems to understand how information relates across domains.

This transforms isolated records into an interconnected model of software delivery.

Instead of querying a single tool, AI systems can reason across multiple systems simultaneously.

Building a Knowledge Graph for Software Delivery

Creating a useful knowledge graph requires more than importing data.

Organizations must establish a process for constructing and maintaining relationships.

The process generally includes several stages.

Entity Extraction

The first step is identifying important objects within the delivery ecosystem.

These may include applications, services, incidents, deployments, users, cloud resources, or security findings.

Metadata Enrichment

Entities become more valuable when supplemented with additional information.

Examples include:

  • Ownership details
  • Team assignments
  • Version information
  • Environment data
  • Compliance classifications
  • Security policies

Relationship Mapping

Relationships define how entities interact.

Understanding who owns a service, which deployment modified it, and what infrastructure supports it is often more valuable than understanding any individual component in isolation.

Query Exposure

Once the graph exists, APIs and query interfaces allow AI agents to retrieve and reason about context dynamically.

At that point, the graph becomes an operational system rather than simply a data repository.

Why Knowledge Graph Projects Fail

Knowledge graphs have existed for years, yet many implementations struggle to deliver value.

According to Mittal, the most common failure is not technical.

It is a failure of use case definition.

Organizations sometimes invest heavily in building sophisticated graph models without clearly identifying the problems they intend to solve.

This creates several risks.

Over-Modeling

Teams create highly detailed ontologies that are technically impressive but provide little practical value.

The result is significant complexity with limited adoption.

Under-Modeling

The opposite problem occurs when relationships are not modeled deeply enough.

Data remains connected only superficially, preventing meaningful reasoning.

Stale Context

A graph is only valuable if it reflects reality.

Outdated relationships and stale metadata quickly reduce the usefulness of AI-driven decision-making.

Successful implementations focus on solving specific operational challenges rather than building graphs for their own sake.

How Knowledge Graphs Enable AI Reasoning

One of the most compelling aspects of knowledge graphs is their ability to support complex reasoning across multiple systems.

During the session, Mittal demonstrated how AI could analyze software delivery pipelines across an organization and identify patterns that would be difficult to discover manually.

Rather than searching individual projects one at a time, the system was able to reason across organizational boundaries.

The AI identified:

  • Pipelines with the highest failure rates
  • Common failure patterns
  • Missing dependencies
  • Configuration issues
  • Potential remediation actions

The system not only surfaced operational problems but also suggested corrective actions based on the relationships captured inside the graph.

This illustrates a broader shift in how AI interacts with enterprise systems.

Instead of responding only to direct questions, AI can begin to understand operational context and assist with diagnosis, prioritization, and decision-making.

Shared Context Across Engineering Disciplines

The value of a knowledge graph extends far beyond DevOps.

Modern software delivery requires collaboration across multiple domains.

DevOps teams care about deployments and reliability.

SecOps teams focus on vulnerabilities and compliance.

FinOps teams analyze cloud spending and resource utilization.

Platform engineering teams manage infrastructure and developer experience.

Traditionally, each group operates within its own set of tools and dashboards.

Knowledge graphs provide a shared context layer that connects these perspectives.

When everyone operates against the same model of services, dependencies, ownership, and operational events, decision-making becomes faster and more consistent.

Governance Becomes a Core AI Requirement

As AI systems gain access to broader organizational context, governance becomes increasingly important.

Enterprise AI cannot operate solely on trust.

Systems require mechanisms for:

  • Role-based access control
  • Policy enforcement
  • Auditability
  • Compliance validation
  • Permission management

Knowledge graphs provide the contextual foundation that allows these controls to be applied consistently.

Without governance, increased context introduces risk.

With governance, context becomes a strategic advantage.

The Future of AI-First Software Delivery

The software industry has spent years building increasingly capable AI models.

The next phase of adoption will depend less on model intelligence and more on organizational context.

The most successful AI systems will not necessarily be those with the largest parameter counts.

They will be the systems that understand services, dependencies, ownership, policies, infrastructure, incidents, and business priorities.

Knowledge graphs provide a mechanism for connecting these elements into a unified model.

As AI moves from assisting developers to actively participating in software delivery workflows, shared context will become essential infrastructure.

Context Is the New Competitive Advantage

Software delivery is becoming increasingly complex.

Organizations operate across dozens of platforms, hundreds of services, and thousands of interconnected components.

AI has the potential to help manage this complexity, but only if it can understand the environment in which it operates.

Knowledge graphs offer a way to transform fragmented organizational knowledge into a connected, queryable system that both humans and AI can reason about.

In an AI-first future, the question will no longer be whether models can generate answers.

The question will be whether they have enough context to generate the right ones.

Database DevOps: Bringing Continuous Delivery to Stateful Applications

Modern software delivery pipelines are remarkably good at deploying stateless applications. Teams can push application updates multiple times a day, automate testing, validate rollouts, and quickly roll back when something goes wrong.

Databases are often a different story.

While application deployments have embraced continuous delivery, database changes frequently remain manual, infrequent, and high-risk. Many organizations that deploy application code daily still schedule database releases monthly or quarterly because schema changes introduce challenges that traditional CI/CD workflows struggle to address.

In his session Database DevOps: CD for Stateful Applications, Stephen Atwell explored how engineering teams can apply modern delivery practices to databases, making stateful systems just as testable, repeatable, and automatable as the applications that depend on them.

Why Databases Remain a Deployment Bottleneck

The core challenge of database delivery is state.

Stateless applications can be replaced, scaled, or rolled back relatively easily because their state lives elsewhere. Databases contain the data that applications depend on, making every structural change potentially risky.

Simple schema updates can become surprisingly complex when applications remain online throughout the deployment process.

Consider a scenario where a single database column needs to be split into multiple fields. During deployment, both the old and new versions of the application may run simultaneously. If each version reads and writes data differently, inconsistencies can emerge immediately.

This challenge often forces teams into maintenance windows, deployment freezes, or highly manual release processes.

As a result, database changes frequently become the limiting factor in otherwise mature continuous delivery environments.

Continuous Delivery Requires Backwards Compatibility

Modern deployment patterns such as blue-green and canary releases depend on running multiple versions of an application simultaneously.

This creates a requirement that many database migrations fail to consider: backwards compatibility.

If version A of an application and version B of an application are both serving traffic, the underlying database must support both versions throughout the transition.

Database changes therefore cannot simply focus on the final desired schema. They must also account for the intermediate states that exist while deployments are in progress.

Successful database delivery requires teams to think about migrations as a series of controlled steps rather than a single change.

The Hidden Complexity of Zero-Downtime Database Migrations

Zero-downtime deployments are relatively common at the application layer. Achieving the same outcome at the database layer is significantly harder.

The challenge becomes particularly apparent when restructuring data.

During the session, Atwell demonstrated a migration that transformed a PostgreSQL table storing serialized JSON data into a properly structured relational schema.

The goal was straightforward: extract fields from a JSON document and store them in dedicated database columns.

The execution, however, required careful planning.

The migration needed to ensure:

  • No downtime
  • No data loss
  • Full backwards compatibility
  • Support for old and new application versions
  • Safe rollback capabilities

Achieving all of these requirements simultaneously demands more than simply writing migration scripts.

Using Database Triggers to Maintain Consistency

One of the key techniques demonstrated during the session involved database triggers.

When introducing new columns, the existing application still expects the original data structure. New application versions, meanwhile, expect the updated schema.

Rather than forcing an immediate switch, synchronization mechanisms can keep both representations aligned.

In the demonstrated migration, triggers ensured that updates to the original JSON field automatically updated the new relational columns.

Additional triggers performed the reverse operation, keeping the original structure synchronized whenever the new schema was modified.

This approach allowed both versions of the application to operate simultaneously while observing the same data.

By maintaining consistency in both directions, teams gain the flexibility needed to deploy, test, validate, and roll back safely.

Large Data Migrations Require More Than Correct SQL

Database migrations often fail not because the migration logic is incorrect, but because operational realities are ignored.

A script that performs well on a development database may behave very differently against production datasets.

Tables may contain millions or billions of rows. Long-running transactions can create lock contention, impact performance, or introduce unexpected downtime.

For this reason, migration strategies must account for scale from the beginning.

Instead of processing entire datasets in a single transaction, modern migration workflows often break work into smaller batches that can execute incrementally and safely.

This reduces risk while allowing migrations to proceed without disrupting production workloads.

AI-Assisted Database Development

One of the more interesting aspects of the demonstration was the use of generative AI to create migration logic.

Rather than manually writing complex PostgreSQL migration code, the schema transformation was generated through natural language prompts.

The generated migration created new columns, built synchronization triggers, and produced the necessary data migration logic.

While AI-generated code still requires validation, it introduces a new workflow for database teams.

Instead of spending hours building migration scripts manually, engineers can focus on reviewing, validating, and testing generated solutions.

The result is a faster iteration cycle while still maintaining governance and operational controls.

Governance Matters as Much as Automation

Automation alone does not make database deployments safe.

Every automated process still requires guardrails.

Throughout the deployment workflow demonstrated during the session, database changes passed through governance checks before being applied.

These checks verified that deployments complied with predefined policies and prevented potentially destructive operations from reaching production environments.

Examples include:

  • Preventing accidental data loss
  • Blocking unsafe schema operations
  • Enforcing deployment policies
  • Creating rollback checkpoints
  • Validating generated SQL before execution

As organizations increase deployment velocity, governance becomes increasingly important because manual review alone cannot scale indefinitely.

Testing Database Changes Against Production Data

One of the biggest challenges in database testing is reproducing production behavior.

Many database issues only appear when migrations encounter real customer data, realistic workloads, or unusual edge cases.

Traditional testing environments often fail to capture these conditions.

To address this challenge, Atwell demonstrated a workflow that clones production data into staging environments before running migration tests.

This approach allows teams to validate schema changes against realistic datasets while still operating within controlled environments.

When combined with automated testing, production-like data significantly improves confidence in deployment outcomes.

Organizations implementing this strategy must ensure that security controls, access policies, and compliance requirements remain consistent between production and staging environments.

Verifying Data Consistency During Deployment

Testing database migrations requires more than simply checking whether a deployment completed successfully.

Teams must verify that data remains consistent throughout the transition.

In the demonstrated workflow, automated tests interacted with both the old and new versions of the application.

Actions performed through one version were immediately validated through the other version.

This process confirmed that both applications continued to observe identical data despite significant schema changes occurring underneath them.

These consistency tests become especially valuable when supporting parallel deployments through blue-green or canary release strategies.

Without this validation, subtle synchronization issues can remain hidden until they affect production users.

Combining Database Migrations with Progressive Delivery

Application delivery practices such as blue-green deployments and canary releases have become common across cloud-native environments.

Database changes can benefit from the same principles.

During the session, schema updates were deployed alongside controlled application rollouts.

In staging environments, blue-green deployments allowed old and new versions to operate simultaneously while automated tests verified compatibility.

In production environments, canary deployments gradually increased traffic to the new version while monitoring system health and behavior.

This progressive approach reduces risk by limiting exposure and creating multiple opportunities to detect issues before they impact all users.

The Future of Database Delivery

For years, databases have been treated as a special case within software delivery pipelines.

Application teams embraced automation while database changes remained manual, infrequent, and operationally risky.

That distinction is beginning to disappear.

Advances in infrastructure automation, Kubernetes-native workflows, AI-assisted development, automated testing, and database-focused CI/CD tooling are making it possible to manage stateful systems using many of the same practices that transformed application delivery.

The goal is not simply faster deployments.

It is creating a delivery process that is more predictable, more repeatable, easier to test, and safer to operate.

Bringing Stateful Applications into Modern CI/CD

Database delivery will always require additional care because data cannot simply be redeployed when something goes wrong.

However, that does not mean databases must remain outside modern delivery practices.

By combining backwards-compatible schema changes, automated testing, governance controls, production-like environments, and progressive deployment strategies, organizations can bring databases into the same continuous delivery workflows that already power their applications.

The result is a more unified software delivery process where both application code and data evolve together, safely and repeatedly, without sacrificing reliability or availability.

entry.content:
Beyond the Toggle: Using Feature Flags to De-Risk Cloud-Native Migrations

Cloud migrations, API rewrites, and large-scale architecture transformations rarely fail because engineers cannot build the new system. More often, they fail because organizations attempt to release too much change at once.

A cloud migration often combines infrastructure changes, application updates, data movement, routing changes, and new operational processes. When all of these elements are introduced simultaneously, teams create a single high-risk event where identifying and recovering from problems becomes significantly more difficult.

During his session, Beyond the Toggle: Feature Flags as Your Cloud-Native Migration Safety Net, Ryan Vila, Americas Advisory Director at Harness, explored how feature management enables organizations to replace risky cutovers with gradual, observable, and reversible migration strategies.

Why Cloud Migrations Create So Much Risk

Many migration initiatives begin with good intentions but quickly become coupled to a traditional release mindset.

Teams often build a new service, deploy it, and then switch all traffic to the new system in a single event. This approach creates several common failure modes.

The first is the "big bang" release. Multiple changes are bundled together and activated simultaneously, making it difficult to isolate the source of problems when issues emerge.

The second challenge is the lack of a practical rollback path. Organizations frequently discover that moving forward is easy, but moving backward is complex, time-consuming, or impossible without disruption.

The third problem is uncontrolled blast radius. If every user is exposed to a migration immediately, even minor issues can quickly become major incidents.

Successful migrations require teams to treat releases differently. Instead of viewing migration as a single event, they need a framework for introducing change gradually while maintaining the ability to observe, pause, and reverse progress when necessary.

The Strangler Fig Pattern in Modern Architectures

One of the most widely adopted migration approaches is the Strangler Fig Pattern, originally popularized by Martin Fowler.

Rather than replacing an existing application all at once, teams introduce new services alongside existing systems and progressively redirect traffic toward the new implementation.

This creates a period where both systems operate in parallel.

The value of this approach is not simply technical flexibility. It provides an opportunity to compare old and new behavior in real-world conditions. Teams can evaluate performance, reliability, cost, and user experience before fully committing to the new architecture.

Once confidence has been established, the legacy service can be retired and the technical debt associated with maintaining parallel systems can be eliminated.

Feature flags provide the control layer that makes this gradual transition practical.

Decoupling Deployment from Release

A key principle of modern feature management is separating deployment from release.

Deployment simply places code into production. Release determines who can actually use it.

By introducing feature flags, engineering teams gain the ability to deploy new functionality without immediately exposing it to every customer.

This enables a progression such as:

  • Internal users and engineering teams
  • Test accounts and synthetic traffic
  • Designated customer groups
  • Small production cohorts
  • Gradually increasing percentages of traffic
  • General availability

Each stage creates an opportunity to validate assumptions before moving forward.

Instead of asking whether the migration succeeds or fails, teams can continuously evaluate whether the migration is producing the desired outcomes.

Progressive Rollouts Reduce Migration Risk

Canary releases and percentage-based rollouts are often discussed in the context of application features, but they are equally valuable for infrastructure and platform transformations.

A small rollout may mean exposing 1% of traffic to a new service.

For another organization, it could mean routing a specific region, customer segment, or internal department through the new architecture.

The exact definition depends on business requirements and risk tolerance.

The important principle is that every increase in exposure should be accompanied by measurement.

A migration that performs well at 5% traffic may behave very differently at 50% or 100%.

Scaling is itself a test, and each expansion should be treated as a validation step rather than an automatic progression.

Measuring More Than Deployment Success

Traditional migration programs often focus on a simple question:

Did the deployment complete successfully?

Modern engineering teams should evaluate migrations against business and operational outcomes.

Performance

Latency, throughput, and response times provide immediate feedback on whether the new implementation delivers improvements over the existing system.

Reliability

Error rates and service-level objectives help determine whether stability improves or deteriorates as traffic increases.

Cost

Cloud migrations are frequently justified by efficiency gains. Measuring infrastructure consumption and operational expenses throughout the rollout helps validate whether expected savings are actually being realized.

Customer Experience

Aggregate metrics can hide problems affecting specific user groups.

Engineering teams should analyze behavior across different cohorts, platforms, regions, and usage patterns to identify issues that may not appear in overall statistics.

A migration that looks healthy at a global level may still introduce significant friction for a specific segment of users.

Monitoring Versus Measurement

One of the most important distinctions highlighted during the session is the difference between monitoring and measurement.

Most organizations already have dashboards, alerts, and observability platforms.

However, observability alone does not necessarily reveal the impact of a specific change.

In production environments, background noise is constant. Small increases in error rates or latency may be difficult to detect when viewed across the entire system.

Measuring from the point of change creates a different perspective.

Instead of asking how the application is behaving overall, teams can evaluate how the newly introduced migration path is performing relative to the baseline.

This approach makes it easier to identify signals that would otherwise be hidden inside broader operational metrics.

The result is faster detection, clearer attribution, and more informed release decisions.

A Real-World Migration Example

Ryan Vila shared an example from Split, the feature management and experimentation platform later acquired by Harness.

The company operated a data processing pipeline responsible for handling massive volumes of customer telemetry.

As customer adoption increased, costs grew linearly with traffic volume. Processing times also became a concern, while customers demanded greater visibility into data quality and ingestion reliability.

The engineering team redesigned the pipeline architecture to support more scalable processing patterns.

Feature flags were used to route traffic between the legacy pipeline and the new implementation.

Rather than performing a risky cutover, traffic could be progressively redirected and evaluated throughout the migration.

The results were substantial:

  • Approximately 80% reduction in operational costs
  • Processing time reduced from roughly 10 hours to 15 minutes
  • Migration completed within a single quarter
  • No customer-facing disruption during rollout
  • Improved visibility and quality controls for customers

The example demonstrates that feature flags are not limited to user-facing features. They can also become a critical mechanism for controlling infrastructure evolution behind the scenes.

Avoiding Common Feature Flag Pitfalls

Feature flags introduce flexibility, but they also require governance.

Stale Flags

Flags created for temporary migrations should not remain indefinitely.

Unused flags increase complexity, create confusion, and may introduce future operational risk.

Untested States

Every flag includes multiple potential states, including fallback behaviors.

Teams should validate each possible outcome rather than testing only the primary path.

Configuration Drift

Flag definitions must remain consistent across staging, production, and disaster recovery environments.

Differences between environments can create unexpected behavior during critical incidents.

Ownership Ambiguity

Every flag should have a clearly defined owner.

When an incident occurs, teams must know who is responsible for evaluating, modifying, or disabling the flag.

Without ownership, response times increase and operational risk grows.

Building a Safer Migration Strategy

Feature flags are often introduced as a way to control application functionality.

Their broader value lies in helping organizations transform how they manage change.

By decoupling deployment from release, engineering teams gain the ability to:

  • Introduce change gradually
  • Reduce blast radius
  • Validate outcomes continuously
  • Roll back safely when needed
  • Measure business and technical impact
  • Modernize systems without disrupting customers

Cloud migrations will always involve risk. The goal is not to eliminate that risk entirely, but to manage it through controlled experimentation and progressive delivery.

Organizations that treat migrations as a series of measurable steps rather than a single release event are better positioned to deliver successful transformations while maintaining reliability, performance, and customer trust.

Resilience Testing Is Non-Negotiable in the Enterprise SDLC

Outages in distributed systems are inevitable, making resilience testing essential in the SDLC. It must be continuous, covering failures, load, and disasters. Delayed validation creates “resilience debt,” increasing risk. A holistic approach combining chaos, load, and disaster recovery testing, along with cross-team collaboration and AI-driven insights, improves reliability and reduces impact.

Modern software delivery has dramatically accelerated. AI-assisted development, automated CI/CD pipelines, and cloud-native architectures now enable teams to deploy software dozens of times per day.

But speed alone does not guarantee reliability.

At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Uma Mukkara, Head of Resilience Testing at Harness and co-creator of LitmusChaos, delivered a clear message: outages are inevitable. In modern distributed systems, assuming your design will always work is not just optimistic, it is risky.

Failure in distributed systems is a mathematical certainty.

That is why resilience testing must become a core, continuous practice in the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC).

The Reality of Inevitable Outages

Even the most reliable cloud providers experience outages.

Examples of unpredictable failures include:

  • Physical disruptions such as drone strikes impacting AWS Middle East data centers
  • Policy or configuration errors triggering cascading outages in platforms like Azure
  • Retry storms and load spikes overwhelming services under unexpected demand

These incidents highlight a critical reality: failure patterns constantly evolve.

A system validated during design may not be resilient against tomorrow’s failure scenarios. Architecture may remain stable, but surrounding failure conditions change continuously.

Resilience cannot rely on assumptions.

Hope is not a strategy. Verification is.

For a broader perspective, explore how chaos engineering, load testing, and disaster recovery testing work together.

What Resilience Really Means

Resilience is often misunderstood as simply keeping systems online.

But uptime alone is not enough.

Resilience is the grace with which systems handle failure and return to an active state.

A resilient system must handle three categories of disruption:

System Failures

Pod crashes, node failures, infrastructure disruptions, and network faults.

Load Conditions

Traffic spikes or sudden demand pushing systems to their limits.

Disasters

Regional outages, multi-AZ failures, and infrastructure loss requiring recovery mechanisms.

Testing only one dimension leaves critical risks undiscovered.

True resilience requires validation across all three.

Continuous Verification in the SDLC

Many organizations still treat resilience as a “day-two problem” handled after deployment.

Others assume that once validated during design, resilience is solved.

Both assumptions are flawed.

Resilience must be continuously verified.

As systems evolve with each release, so do their failure modes. Effective teams:

  • Test resilience continuously
  • Verify resilience with every delivery
  • Document results across releases

This shifts resilience testing into the outer loop of the SDLC, alongside functional and performance testing.

Instead of reacting to production incidents, teams proactively identify weaknesses before customers experience them.

Understanding Resilience Debt

Resilience debt is similar to technical debt.

When teams delay resilience validation, they accumulate hidden risks.

Over time, this debt compounds.

When failure inevitably occurs, business impact scales with the amount of unresolved resilience debt.

The solution is consistent expansion of resilience testing coverage.

As testing matures over time, teams gain:

  • Better system feedback
  • Earlier risk detection
  • Reduced likelihood of severe outages

A Holistic Approach to Resilience Testing

Resilience testing should not exist in silos.

Many organizations separate:

  • Chaos testing
  • Load testing
  • Disaster recovery validation

But real-world failures often occur at their intersection.

Examples:

  • Resource bottlenecks emerging only under combined load and failure conditions
  • Chaos experiments reused for disaster recovery validation
  • Combined chaos and load testing revealing system limits

A holistic approach integrates:

  • Chaos Engineering
  • Load Testing
  • Disaster Recovery (DR) Validation

Learn more in the Harness Resilience Testing documentation.

Collaboration Across Teams

Resilience testing requires cross-functional collaboration.

Key contributors include:

  • Developers
  • QA engineers
  • SREs
  • Platform teams

Many organizations already share infrastructure but run isolated experiments.

By coordinating efforts, teams can:

  • Reuse testing environments
  • Share chaos experiments
  • Validate DR workflows more frequently
  • Improve overall efficiency

Resilience improves significantly when teams share assets instead of operating in silos.

The Role of AI in Resilience Testing

As systems grow more complex, determining what to test and when becomes challenging.

Large organizations may have hundreds of possible experiments.

Agentic AI systems can help prioritize testing by analyzing:

  • Incident data
  • CI/CD pipeline history
  • Infrastructure configuration
  • Operational documentation

AI can recommend:

  • Relevant chaos experiments
  • Appropriate load scenarios
  • Timely disaster recovery tests

This ensures teams run the right tests at the right time without overwhelming engineering capacity.

A Unified Platform for Resilience Testing

Harness has expanded its chaos engineering capabilities into a unified platform: Harness Resilience Testing.

This platform enables teams to:

  • Design chaos experiments
  • Run load tests
  • Validate disaster recovery workflows
  • Observe system risk patterns

All within a single environment.

This unified approach provides a single pane of glass for identifying and tracking resilience risks across the SDLC.

Resilience Is a Core Practice for Modern SRE Teams

Resilience testing is not optional.

Outages will happen. Infrastructure will fail. Dependencies will break.

What matters is whether systems have been continuously validated against those failures.

As resilience testing coverage increases:

  • Feedback improves
  • Risk visibility grows
  • Business impact decreases

In modern software delivery, resilience is no longer just a reliability practice.

It is a core discipline of the enterprise SDLC.

entry.title: Secure by Default: Why AI-Driven Delivery Needs a Rethink
entry.summary: Why fast, AI-powered delivery demands secure-by-default pipelines.
entry.content:
By Dewan Ahmed

Software delivery has been accelerating for more than a decade, and the arrival of AI has pushed us into an entirely new velocity class. Code generation, configuration scaffolding, infrastructure suggestions, remediation hints, and deployment decisions now involve AI. It participates in every stage of the delivery pipeline.

On the surface, this feels like progress. Faster delivery, fewer bottlenecks, happier teams.
But a closer look reveals something more complicated.

The Gap Between Speed and Safety

Most modern pipelines were designed for a world where humans made the important decisions, such as writing code, reviewing changes, crafting configurations, and evaluating risks. AI changed that dynamic. It introduced automation that moves faster than traditional security practices can respond to.

The result is a widening gap between the speed at which we can ship and the safety at which we can ship.

Here are a few of the challenges teams are already feeling today.

1. AI is amplifying existing weaknesses

If your base images are outdated, your tests barely cover your codebase, or your deployment strategy lacks guardrails, AI does not fix these issues. It accelerates them.

Pipelines automate mistakes with the same enthusiasm they automate features.

2. The threat surface has shifted

The most common AI failures today are not the classic vulnerabilities we are used to scanning for.

Instead, organizations are seeing issues such as:

  • prompt injection
  • model jailbreaking
  • vulnerable AI-generated code
  • behavior-driven exploits
  • configuration drift caused by AI tools

These attacks target behavior and reasoning, not code structure.

3. Delivery is faster, but security has not kept up

AI-assisted workflows generate code, configurations, and infrastructure definitions at machine speed. Most security models still rely on manual reviews, point-in-time scans, or human approval gates.

This mismatch means misconfigurations are no longer slow, human-scale mistakes. They have become automated hazards.

4. Developers are not set up for AI-era security

Most developers have little or no training in AI security or AI threat modeling, yet we expect them to recognize model manipulation, unsafe outputs, and subtle behavioral failures in AI-generated artifacts. The expectations do not match the support we give them.

These challenges will define the next era of DevSecOps. If you want to hear about a practical four-pillar framework for secure-by-default AI-driven delivery, join my keynote at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025.

entry.title: Where software expects failure and keeps running
entry.content:
Cloud native started as a promise.

You know the one. Faster deployments. Infinite scale. Fewer problems. More sleep.

Somewhere along the way, it turned into Kubernetes YAML, surprise cloud bills, fifteen dashboards, and a deep emotional relationship with latency. Growth.

Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 is here for everyone living that reality.

This is a big one. Seventy plus talks across Kubernetes, microservices, APIs, data, observability, security, AI, scaling, and all the tools that somehow became “essential”. From cloud testing without the wait to running ultra budget workloads for pennies, this conference covers the whole spectrum from scrappy to enterprise-grade.

AI is everywhere, naturally. Cloud-native LLMs, predictive analytics, AI-powered fraud detection, recommendation systems, digital twins, and AI-driven operations show up across industries like healthcare, finance, insurance, retail, manufacturing, and entertainment. There’s plenty of “this is cool”, and also a healthy dose of “here’s how this breaks in production”.

Kubernetes gets a lot of love. Real-world stories about running clusters at scale, improving uptime, reducing costs, simplifying connectivity, and making microservices behave. There are also talks questioning assumptions, defending simpler architectures, and reminding us that not every problem needs twelve services and a service mesh.

Security, resilience, and observability are baked throughout the program. Secrets management, zero trust, multi-cloud monitoring, chaos engineering, disaster recovery, and cost optimization all make an appearance. Because cloud native is not just about shipping faster, it’s about surviving success.

If your job involves containers, clouds, APIs, data pipelines, or explaining to someone why the architecture diagram looks like that, this one’s for you. Cloud native is powerful, messy, and still very much evolving.

Bring curiosity. And maybe your favorite kubectl alias.

entry.title: Introducing uncertainty before users feel it
entry.content:
Chaos engineering sounds dramatic. Like you’re about to pull cables out of walls and see who panics first.

In reality, it’s much more thoughtful than that. Mostly.

Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 is all about building systems that keep working even when the universe decides to be uncooperative. Network hiccups, failing dependencies, cloud outages, bad configs, expired certificates, and that one service nobody remembers owning. You know the drill.

This conference digs into how teams actually test resilience. Fault injection, chaos experiments, failure scenarios, and learning what really happens under pressure. There are talks on microservices, event-driven architectures, cloud databases, APIs, and what breaks first when things scale faster than expected.

AI shows up here too, because of course it does. Expect sessions on AI model monitoring, AI-driven chaos experiments, and using machine learning to detect issues before users do. Some talks focus on reliability. Others focus on making sure automation doesn’t confidently lead you in the wrong direction.

But chaos isn’t just technical. A big part of the program looks at people, culture, and mindset. Platform teams, leadership, communication, and why throwing more tools at a problem doesn’t magically make systems resilient. Spoiler: humans are still involved.

You’ll also find real-world case studies across cloud, mobile, security, finance, healthcare, and enterprise platforms. From testing disaster recovery to breaking things safely in production, this is chaos engineering where the goal is learning, not drama.

If you like understanding how systems fail before they fail loudly, this one’s for you. Controlled chaos beats surprise chaos. Every time.

entry.title: One language, countless domains
entry.content:
Python keeps being that language people “grow out of”.

And then somehow keep using forever.

It’s in data, web, AI, cloud, healthcare, security, automation, embedded systems, and probably running something important you forgot about. Conf42 Python 2025 leans fully into that reality.

This conference covers a lot of ground. There are talks on FastAPI, GraphQL microservices, async workflows, packaging without pain, and scaling Python systems that actually survive production. You’ll also find deep dives into concurrency, distributed file systems, performance tuning, and when Python absolutely should not be doing everything by itself.

AI is, unsurprisingly, everywhere. From AI agents and LLM-powered applications to code review, fraud detection, recommendation systems, and data quality management, Python sits right in the middle of modern machine learning workflows. Some sessions focus on building smarter systems. Others focus on keeping them accurate, explainable, and under control.

There’s plenty beyond AI too. Python in healthcare, finance, IoT, security, and cloud platforms shows up across the schedule. Topics range from embedded device security and zero trust to data warehousing, analytics with Streamlit, and high-throughput financial systems handling millions of events per second.

You’ll also find talks that are just… very Python. Dunder methods. Packaging for busy people. Mixing Python with C++ when performance really matters. And even a reminder that Python can make music, not just dashboards.

If Python is part of your day job, your side projects, or your personality at this point, this one’s for you. It’s practical, wide-ranging, and very comfortable with the fact that Python refuses to stay in one lane.

entry.title: From commit to customer at speed
entry.content:
Every year someone declares DevOps “done”, “dead”, or “just how things are now”.

And every year, DevOps quietly adds five more responsibilities, a few new tools, and at least one AI-powered opinion about how you should be doing your job.

Conf42 DevOps 2025 embraces that reality.

This conference is packed. Fifty plus talks across culture, cloud, data, security, testing, observability, incidents, scaling, performance, AI, LLMs, and whatever category your current problem accidentally falls into. If it touches delivery, operations, or keeping systems alive, it’s probably here.

AI shows up everywhere. From generative AI in cloud-native DevOps to AI-assisted monitoring, fraud detection, data pipelines, testing, and even build failure automation. Some talks focus on the promise. Others focus on trust, accuracy, and what happens when AI confidently gives you the wrong answer at scale.

But it’s not all machines. There are plenty of sessions on culture, leadership, impostor syndrome, quiet engineers, and the human side of running complex systems. Because no amount of automation fixes burnout, unclear ownership, or “we’ll just ship it and see”.

You’ll also find deep dives into Kubernetes, serverless, observability, security, incident response, healthcare platforms, and large-scale migrations. From zero to millions of users. From flaky tests to resilient systems. From “why is this slow” to “oh… that’s why”.

If DevOps is your job, your background, or your current identity crisis, this one’s for you. It’s messy, evolving, and still very much not finished.

See you there.

entry.title: Where the physical world joins the internet
entry.content:
Once upon a time, the internet lived safely inside computers.

Now it’s in cars, factories, medical devices, oil pipelines, kiosks, fridges, traffic systems, and that one sensor nobody remembers installing but everyone is afraid to touch. Welcome to IoT.

Conf42 Internet of Things 2024 is here to make sense of that world.

This conference covers the full IoT stack, from edge devices and connectivity to cloud platforms, analytics, security, and automation. You’ll find talks on robotics, industrial IoT, real-time analytics, digital twins, Kubernetes at the edge, and what happens when AI meets thousands of devices that never sleep.

AI is everywhere, obviously. Expect sessions on explainable AI for IoT, AI-driven cloud architectures, predictive analytics, automation, and using machine learning to turn massive streams of device data into something resembling a decision. There’s also plenty on observability, telemetry, and figuring out what’s actually going on when things stop behaving.

The use cases go wide. Healthcare, fintech, automotive, logistics, energy, retail, and smart infrastructure all show up. From contact tracing and crisis management to autonomous vehicles and supply chain optimization, this is IoT in the real world, not just diagrams on slides.

Security and reliability get their share of attention too. Identity federation, zero trust, blockchain, multi-layered defenses, and securing connected ecosystems where failure is not an option and “just reboot it” is rarely acceptable.

If your job involves devices, data, clouds, or explaining to someone why a sensor stopped reporting at 3 AM, this one’s for you. IoT is messy, powerful, and very much alive. Let’s talk about it.

entry.title: When security stops being a checkpoint
entry.summary: And becomes part of the workflow
entry.content:
DevSecOps is that thing everyone agrees is important and then quietly argues about in pull requests.

Should security shift left? Should it shift everywhere? Should it maybe stop breaking the build five minutes before a release? Big questions. Strong feelings.

Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 is here to unpack all of that.

This one goes wide and deep. There are talks on securing infrastructure, web applications, APIs, and Kubernetes clusters that absolutely did not ask to be exposed to the internet. You’ll hear about secrets management, Git leaks, identity federation, policy as code, and why credentials have a habit of showing up where they really shouldn’t.

AI is very much in the mix. Expect sessions on AIOps, alert noise reduction, AI-driven security assessments, explainable AI, and the slightly terrifying reality of AI being very interested in your secrets. There’s even a panel dedicated to that exact concern, because of course there is.

Beyond tools, the conference also digs into culture, governance, and the human side of security. Soft skills, leadership, compliance, resilience, and what DevSecOps looks like in healthcare, finance, supply chains, and other environments where mistakes are extra expensive.

You’ll find practical talks on Terraform, GitOps, cloud databases, internal developer platforms, and shifting from monoliths to microservices without everything catching fire. There’s also room for bigger conversations about trust, accountability, and what “secure by default” actually means in real teams.

If your job lives somewhere between shipping fast and sleeping at night, this one’s worth your time. DevSecOps isn’t getting simpler, but at least you don’t have to figure it out alone.

entry.title: Teaching machines by example and constraint
entry.content:
At some point this year, a lot of us realized we’re no longer just writing code.

We’re negotiating. With models. Politely. Repeatedly. Sometimes aggressively. Sometimes with emojis. Sometimes with “no, seriously, do it like this”.

Welcome to prompt engineering.

Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 is all about that strange new layer between humans and machines, where wording matters, context is everything, and a single sentence can be the difference between brilliance and absolute nonsense.

There are talks on securing prompts, preventing injection attacks, and making sure your AI doesn’t spill secrets the moment you look away. Others dig into orchestration, agents completing missions, and turning prompts into actual systems that do useful work instead of just vibing.

You’ll also find plenty of real-world use cases. Healthcare. Retail. Finance. HR. Education. Cloud platforms. Testing. Even SRE perspectives on keeping AI-driven systems reliable when prompts start getting creative at 2 AM.

Some sessions go deep into LLMs, multimodal models, embeddings, vectors, and feedback loops. Others take a more human approach, exploring ethics, bias, hallucinations, and what it means to trust AI output when the stakes are higher than a funny chatbot reply.

If you’ve ever thought “why did the model do that” or “how do I get this thing to behave”, this conference is probably for you. And if prompt engineering has quietly become part of your job title, well… you’re definitely in the right place.
